### Segment 2 — The Good Intention
After World War II, many American and European cities faced acute housing shortages as returning veterans and industrial workers competed for limited units. Local officials watched rents climb sharply in tight markets and concluded that price ceilings would prevent displacement and maintain social stability. In New York, the 1943 federal rent-control order and its local successors were defended as temporary measures to protect tenants from wartime profiteering.

sections.lesson:
### Segment 6 — The Lesson
Price ceilings on a durable good with long production lags tend to shrink the stock of that good over time. When rules create large windfall gains for current occupants, those beneficiaries become a durable political constituency that resists later adjustment. Complex urban housing markets transmit the effects of a single intervention through multiple channels—maintenance, conversion, mobility, and new supply—so the net result is rarely confined to the targeted price.

The legislation that became No Child Left Behind was shaped by a bipartisan coalition that included President George W. Bush, Representative John Boehner, and Senator Edward Kennedy. Its central goal was to close long-standing achievement gaps between low-income students, students of color, and their more advantaged peers. Earlier federal efforts such as the 1965 Elementary and Secondary Education Act had distributed money with few requirements to show results.
